title: Oil Prices Surge 16% in a Week as US-Iran War Escalation Threatens Strait of Hormuz Shutdown
excerpt: Brent crude hits $88 as seven straight nights of US strikes on Iran, tanker attacks, and a potential Red Sea closure push oil markets toward crisis levels.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Brent crude surged to $88.10 per barrel, marking a 16% weekly increase.
  • U.S. strikes on Iran escalated, with Tehran retaliating against regional infrastructure.
  • Strait of Hormuz tanker traffic has plummeted, falling below 50% of pre-war levels.
  • India banned its seafarers from Hormuz voyages after two nationals were killed.
  • U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve is at its lowest since April 1983, at 316.5 million barrels.

  • Brent crude settled at $88.10 per barrel on Friday, its highest since mid-June, with both benchmarks gaining about 16% for the week.
  • The U.S. carried out seven consecutive nights of strikes on Iran; Tehran retaliated by hitting infrastructure in Kuwait, Qatar, and threatening to close the Red Sea through Houthi proxies.
  • Gulf crude flows through the Strait of Hormuz have fallen below 50% of pre-war levels, with Iran targeting vessels transiting the waterway.
  • India has banned its seafarers from Hormuz voyages after two nationals were killed; over 15,000 Indian crew members remain stranded west of the strait.

Oil prices posted their biggest weekly gain in months as the escalating war between the United States and Iran drove fears of a full shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz, the chokepoint through which roughly a fifth of global crude supplies flow.

Brent crude futures settled $3.87 higher at $88.10 per barrel on Friday, while West Texas Intermediate rose $3.54 to $82.49. Both benchmarks gained about 16% for the week, according to Reuters, with Brent on track for a third consecutive weekly gain.

Seven Nights of Strikes

U.S. Central Command confirmed Friday that American forces carried out their seventh consecutive night of strikes on Iran, targeting surveillance sites, military logistics infrastructure, underground weapons storage, and maritime capabilities. More than 50,000 U.S. service members are deployed across the Middle East.

Iran expanded its retaliation beyond its immediate borders. Tehran struck a power and desalination plant in Kuwait on Friday, fired missiles at Qatar, and for the first time in the war launched strikes at a U.S. base in Syria. Iran also pressed the Houthi rebel group in Yemen to threaten closure of the Bab el-Mandeb strait at the mouth of the Red Sea — Saudi Arabia’s main alternative route for oil exports bypassing the Gulf.

Hormuz Flows Near Zero

The situation in the Strait of Hormuz has deteriorated sharply. Tanker traffic through the waterway has dropped close to zero, according to OilPrice.com, despite a brief recovery after a ceasefire deal in mid-June that had boosted Gulf exports to 12 million barrels per day in early July — the highest since before the war began in February.

That ceasefire collapsed on July 7 over disputes about the strait’s administration. Iran resumed attacks on commercial vessels, and the United States reinstated its naval blockade of Iranian ports, redirecting at least two commercial ships since the blockade resumed.

“If more tankers come under fire and become damaged, we’re going to see oil prices continue to move up as shipowners simply refuse to enter the Persian Gulf.”

— Andrew Lipow, Lipow Oil Associates

Strategic Reserve at 43-Year Low

The supply picture is increasingly strained. The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve fell to 316.5 million barrels in the week ending July 10 — its lowest level since April 1983 and only 44% of capacity. Total U.S. crude inventories including the SPR sit near the October 1984 low.

China’s crude imports have plunged 41% year-on-year in June to 7.12 million barrels per day, the lowest since October 2016, as disrupted Middle Eastern supplies compound weakening domestic demand.

India’s Seafarer Ban

India has banned the deployment of its seafarers on ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz after two Indian nationals were killed in regional attacks. Maritime unions warn that more than 15,000 Indian crew members remain stranded west of the embattled waterway.

The oil price surge has broader implications for India, the world’s third-largest oil importer. Higher crude prices increase the country’s import bill, pressure the rupee, and risk reigniting inflation that the Reserve Bank of India has been working to contain.

What’s Next

Goldman Sachs warned this week that renewed tanker attacks are pushing oil risk higher, revising its earlier view that flows would normalize by month’s end. The bank now sees significant upside risk if fighting continues to restrict Hormuz passage.

For now, the market is pricing in disruption rather than resolution. As one portfolio manager told Bloomberg: “We only had that short-term peace when energy executives were warning that we’ve been drawing down inventories. There’s really not a lot of slack left in the system.”
